paras: The lynching at Stony Creek was the hanging of an unnamed Native American man, called only "an Indian" in the press, by a mob at Stony Creek, thirty miles west of Colusa, California, on the night of April 24, 1882. He had been arrested and was in a constable's charge when the mob took him and hanged him. A single dispatch from Colusa carried the story across the country, and roundups of the week's lynchings repeated it in a line.

According to the Colusa dispatch, the man had threatened the life of J. M. Pugh, described as "a prominent farmer." The same dispatch said he "had been engaged in one murder" and was "a desperate character," without naming the murder or its victim. These charges came only from the dispatch, and no paper reported a court proceeding against him.

The man had been arrested and was being held by a constable at the time of the lynching. On the night of April 24, which the Southern Herald gave as a Monday, a mob took him from the constable and hanged him. The reports do not say where along Stony Creek he was killed, how many men made up the mob, or whether the constable resisted.
No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and the victim's name was never printed.

The dispatch was dated Colusa, April 27, and went out by wire from San Francisco, appearing on April 28 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Daily Los Angeles Herald, the New-York Tribune and other papers. Headlines labeled the victim only by race: "An Indian Lynched" in Los Angeles, "An Indian Hung by a Mob" in Eureka, and "One Indian Gone" in the Wheeling Register. Every version repeated the dispatch's account of the man as a threat and a "desperate character," and none questioned the hanging or the mob's taking him from an officer.

Shorter versions spread through the weekly press into May. A "Condensed Telegrams" brief, printed in the Bolivar Bulletin and the Richmond Democrat, called him "a bad man generally." Roundups of lynchings, such as one in the Bourbon News, reduced the event to "An Indian murderer was lynched on Stormy Creek," turning the dispatch's allegation into a label and misprinting the place name. The Bourbon News and Somerset Press listed it with two other lynchings of the same days and closed, "A good record for one day."
Most versions named the threatened farmer J. M. Pugh, while the Wheeling Register printed "J. M. Hugh" and the condensed wire did not name him.

bases: A mob took an arrested man from a constable and hanged him (A3, A2).

A mob hanged a prisoner it took from a constable, on the stated grounds that he had threatened a farmer's life and been engaged in a murder (A3, A2); a 'mob' is taken as three or more though no number is given. The victim was described as an Indian, not as Black (A3).
Every report traces to one Colusa dispatch of April 27 relayed from San Francisco (A3, A1, A2); no independent local account was found.

framing.detail: California and eastern dailies ran the Colusa dispatch under headlines like 'An Indian Lynched' and 'An Indian Hung by a Mob', repeating its characterization of the victim without comment.
The Wheeling Register headed it 'One Indian Gone'; weekly roundups called him 'An Indian murderer' and closed 'A good record for one day.'
The Bolivar Bulletin's brief called him 'a bad man generally' within a list of condensed telegrams.
